elements.quote: This systematic review provides a comprehensive overview of ER behavioral observation and physiological measures of children and adolescents, including their theoretical embedding and psychometric properties.
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly labels the work as a systematic review.

elements.quote: This systematic review provides a comprehensive overview of ER behavioral observation and physiological measures of children and adolescents, including their theoretical embedding and psychometric properties.
elements.reason: The abstract states the main objective: to provide a comprehensive overview of ER behavioral and physiological measures, their theoretical grounding, and psychometric properties.

elements.quote: We included empirical studies assessing ER as an outcome variable in children and adolescents aged 0-15 years using at least one behavioral or physiological ER measure. Studies on secondary literature were excluded.
elements.reason: The abstract specifies inclusion criteria (empirical studies, ER outcome, age 0-15, behavioral or physiological measures) and excludes secondary literature.

elements.quote: we conducted a systematic literature search in PubMed, PsycINFO, Psyndex plus, and Web of Science without language restrictions.
elements.reason: The abstract lists the information sources (databases) searched but does not report the date when each source was last searched (last search date is provided elsewhere in the manuscript, not in the abstract).
The abstract does not describe the methods or tools used to assess risk of bias in the included studies.

elements.quote: Measurement types, theoretical grounding, and psychometric properties (reliability, validity, objectivity) were extracted and compared across age groups using descriptive statistics and chi-square tests.
elements.reason: The abstract states the analytical/synthesis methods used (extraction, descriptive statistics, chi-square tests) to present and compare results.

elements.quote: A total of 516 studies met inclusion criteria.
elements.reason: The abstract reports the total number of included studies (516) and summarizes study characteristics (e.g., types of measures, percentages), but it does not report the total number of participants across the included studies.

elements.quote: Only 5% reported validity evidence, 62% reliability, and 20% objectivity. Few studies referenced an ER definition or empirically tested an ER model. LAB-TAB and Delay of Gratification tasks were the most common behavioral observation measures, whereas RSA and EEG dominated physiological measures. Behavioral observation was more frequently used in younger children, whereas physiological measures were more common in older children ( p < .001; V = .37). Most studies focused on the regulation of negative emotions (91%), and 90% relied on a single ER measure.
elements.reason: The abstract presents main results for the principal outcomes (reporting rates of psychometric properties, common measures, age-related differences) with study counts (total studies) and percentages.

elements.quote: Meta-analyses were performed in R (version 4.4.1) using the meta package (Fig. 2).
elements.reason: A meta-analysis was conducted (evidence elsewhere in the manuscript), but the abstract does not report any summary estimate or confidence/credible interval as required when a meta-analysis is performed.

elements.quote: Behavioral observation was more frequently used in younger children, whereas physiological measures were more common in older children ( p < .001; V = .37).
elements.reason: The abstract reports a comparison between groups (younger vs older children) and indicates the direction of the effect (which group more frequently used each measurement type).
The abstract does not provide a brief summary of important limitations of the included evidence (limitations are reported in the manuscript but not in the abstract).

elements.quote: ER measurement in children and adolescents is characterized by limited psychometric reporting and insufficient theoretical integration. This review provides an overview of available methods and their psychometric properties, facilitating the selection of appropriate measures for future research. Greater emphasis on validity,
elements.reason: The abstract offers a general interpretation of the results and states important implications for future research (need for better psychometric reporting and validity emphasis).
The abstract does not specify the primary source of funding for the review (funding information appears in the PRISMA checklist table but is not present in the abstract).

elements.quote: The review protocol was pre-registered at PROSPERO (ID: CRD42021266452, ...)
elements.reason: Although the manuscript reports registration and registration number elsewhere, the abstract itself does not provide the register name and registration number as required.

elements.quote: The meta-analytic findings highlight substantial gaps in the reporting of psychometric properties across the literature. A considerable proportion of studies (39%) did not report any psychometric information, meaning that the meta-analytic results were necessarily based on a subset of studies. ... Evidence on reliability and validity, particularly discriminant validity and test-retest reliability, remains largely derived from adult populations and questionnaire-based measures [26, 28, 33, 224], with comparatively limited data available for behavioral observations and physiological measures in children.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly describes the current state of knowledge and several important uncertainties/gaps (e.g., substantial non-reporting of psychometric properties, reliance on adult/questionnaire evidence, limited data for behavioral and physiological measures).

elements.quote: Valid and reliable ER measures are needed to develop models for mental health promotion and treatment. This systematic review provides a comprehensive overview of ER behavioral observation and physiological measures of children and adolescents, including their theoretical embedding and psychometric properties.
elements.reason: The abstract states the importance and need for the review (need for valid/reliable ER measures and providing a comprehensive overview), thus explaining why the review was conducted.

No retrieved evidence describes existing similar systematic reviews or explains the need for the current review relative to prior reviews; no citations or statements about updates/replications were found in the provided text.
The review concerns measurement methods for emotion regulation (behavioral and physiological measures), not intervention effects; thus a mechanism of action for an intervention is not applicable.
The review does not evaluate complex interventions or delivery contexts, so a logic model of intervention components and outcomes is not applicable.

elements.quote: The primary outcome was the reporting of psychometric properties in behavioral and physiological ER measures.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly states the primary outcome of the review, which constitutes an explicit statement of the review's objective/question (i.e., to assess reporting of psychometric properties in behavioral and physiological ER measures).

elements.quote: Studies were included according to the PICOS criteria [177]. Eligible studies included participants from birth to 15 years and 11 months. Studies were required to use at least one ER measurement and report ER as an outcome variable. Both studies with and without group comparisons were eligible.
elements.reason: The review addresses measurement and reporting of emotion regulation outcomes rather than effects of interventions; the inclusion criteria permit studies with and without group comparisons, indicating this is not a review of intervention effects requiring PICO-formulated planned comparisons.

elements.quote: The search was updated continuously until 13.09.2024.
elements.reason: A date is explicitly reported indicating when the search was last updated/continued (13.09.2024).

elements.quote: We used topic-specific databases PubMed (including MEDLINE; Ovid), PsycINFO (including PsycArticles; EBSCOhost), Psyndex plus (EBSCOhost) and Web of Science (Thomson Reuters, Clarivate Analytics) for adjoining disciplines.
elements.reason: Database names and platforms/interfaces are reported (e.g., PubMed/MEDLINE via Ovid, PsycINFO via EBSCOhost, Web of Science/Clarivate), but available coverage dates for each database are not provided.
No study registers, regulatory databases, or online repositories are reported as being searched in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: In contrast to the previously pre-registered search strategy, the Google Scholar database was excluded due to the large number of records retrieved, which exceeded the feasible scope of screening. Instead, Psyndex Plus was included as an additional database.
elements.reason: Names of some online sources/databases are provided (e.g., Google Scholar excluded, Psyndex Plus included), but no URLs are reported for websites/search engines, so the requirement to report names and URLs is only partially met.
The evidence does not report contacting organisations or manufacturers to identify studies; only that study authors were contacted for full texts.

elements.quote: For studies with unavailable full-texts, authors were contacted or articles purchased.
elements.reason: The type of individuals contacted (study authors) is explicitly reported.

elements.quote: Additionally, manual reference checks and citation tracking in the Social Science Citation Index were conducted.
elements.reason: The methods used for examining references are described (manual reference checks and citation tracking), but the specific types of reference lists examined (e.g., reference lists of included studies, reviews) are not specified.

elements.quote: Additionally, manual reference checks and citation tracking in the Social Science Citation Index were conducted.
elements.reason: The citation index/platform used for citation tracking (Social Science Citation Index) is reported, and the flow diagram (Fig. 2) visually shows forward and backward search counts; however, the seed reports used for citation searching and the dates of those specific citation searches are not reported.
elements.confidence_note_image: Figure (text_14 image) shows 'Forward Search (n = 90) / Backward Search (n = 240)' for studies with behavioral observations and physiological measures (visual evidence of counts), supporting that forward/backward citation searching was performed but not giving search dates or seed report identifiers.

elements.reason: No journals or conference proceedings consulted (with names, dates covered, or search methods) are reported in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: Search Terms: 'emotion* regulat*' OR 'emotion* management' OR 'affect* regulat*' If there is no age selection by the searching machine, we add: AND'child*' OR 'infan*' OR 'neonatal' OR 'newborn' OR 'bab*' OR 'toddler' OR'preschooler' OR 'preschool*' OR 'schoolchildren' OR 'pupils' OR 'youth' OR'young' OR 'teen' OR 'kid*' OR 'juvenile' OR 'adolescen*'
elements.reason: Search terms are provided (Appendix File 3) showing the PubMed search terms and age terms, but the full, exact search strategies as actually run for each database (adapted strings for PsycINFO, Psyndex, Web of Science, etc.) are not shown in the retrieved evidence for every source. The manuscript refers to a PubMed strategy in Appendix File 3 but complete per-database strategies are not fully presented in the supplied evidence.

elements.quote: No publication date limits were applied. In contrast to the previously pre-registered search strategy, the Google Scholar database was excluded due to the large number of records retrieved, which exceeded the feasible scope of screening.
elements.reason: The evidence reports that no publication date limits were applied and documents the exclusion of Google Scholar with justification. However, other possible search limits (e.g., language, study type, human subjects) are not described in the supplied evidence, so description and justification of all search limits are only partially reported.

elements.quote: The search strategy was piloted in PubMed and adapted for each database (search strategy for PubMed, Appendix, File 3). In contrast to the previously pre-registered search strategy, the Google Scholar database was excluded due to the large number of records retrieved, which exceeded the feasible scope of screening. Instead, Psyndex Plus was included as an additional database.
elements.reason: The manuscript states that the PubMed strategy was adapted for each database and documents an adaptation (excluding Google Scholar, adding Psyndex Plus), but it does not cite any published search approaches or filters nor give detailed descriptions of adaptations from published filters in the supplied evidence.
No information in the supplied evidence indicates the use of natural-language processing or text-analysis tools to identify or refine search terms.
The supplied evidence does not report any tools used to translate search strings between sources.

elements.quote: The search strategy was piloted in PubMed and adapted for each database (search strategy for PubMed, Appendix, File 3).
elements.reason: The search was piloted in PubMed, which indicates some preliminary testing, but no detailed description of a validation process or validation studies is provided in the supplied evidence.
There is no evidence in the supplied material of any peer review of the search strategy (e.g., PRESS) or description of such a process.
The supplied evidence does not indicate that the search structure was not based on PICO, nor does it describe a final conceptual structure or the explorations used to develop it.
The provided evidence describes the data extraction tool and extracted data items (text_9) but does not state how many reviewers collected data from each report or who performed the data extraction.

Although screening and full-text assessment are described as being done independently (text_13), there is no explicit statement about whether multiple data collectors performed data extraction and whether they worked independently.

elements.quote: Discrepancies (29%) were resolved through discussion and consensus. ... Disagreements were resolved by consensus. ... Any discrepancies in ratings were discussed until consensus was reached.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly describes processes used to resolve disagreements (discussion and consensus) for screening, full-text assessment, and risk-of-bias ratings (text_13).

No information is provided about processes used to obtain or confirm data from study investigators; the evidence mentions exclusions when researchers could not be contacted but does not describe procedures for contacting or confirming data.

elements.quote: Records excluded by automation tool (n = 7336) by human (n = 4143)
elements.reason: The PRISMA flow diagram (figure in text_14) shows that an automation tool was used to exclude records, indicating use of automation in the process, but no details are provided about the automation tool, its use, training, or validation.

While the manuscript notes exclusions of four articles due to Japanese language and states no language restrictions were applied (text_12 and text_7), it does not describe methods used to translate articles for data collection.
No information is provided about software used to extract data from figures; the data extraction description (text_9) lists extracted items but not any software for figure extraction.

The manuscript does not describe decision rules for selecting data from multiple reports or for resolving inconsistent information across reports; the evidence only states that included studies used different ER measures and notes exclusions, without describing selection rules.

elements.quote: The primary outcome was the reporting of psychometric properties in behavioral and physiological ER measures.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly lists a primary outcome (reporting of psychometric properties for behavioral and physiological ER measures), but it does not provide a comprehensive list and definitions of all outcome domains sought beyond this primary outcome.
No text specifies the time frame(s) of measurement for each outcome domain or time points at which outcomes were measured.
The manuscript does not state whether all results compatible with each outcome domain (e.g., all measures, time points, analyses) were sought.
There is no description of a process used to select among multiple compatible results within outcome domains when not all results were sought.

elements.quote: Modifications to the pre-registered eligibility criteria and search strategy were made due to an initially large number of hits (over 35,000).
elements.reason: Although modifications to eligibility criteria and search strategy are reported, the manuscript does not report any changes specifically to outcome-domain inclusion, definitions, or their importance with rationales; therefore this required detail is missing.
No changes to processes for selecting results within eligible outcome domains (or rationales for such changes) are reported in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: The primary outcome was the reporting of psychometric properties in behavioral and physiological ER measures.
elements.reason: The manuscript identifies the outcome considered most important for interpretation (reporting of psychometric properties for behavioral and physiological ER measures) which indicates prioritisation for the review's conclusions.

elements.quote: Extracted data comprised study identification, study and measurement characteristics (study design, publication type), sample characteristics (age, gender, ethnicity, child/family characteristics), definition/model of ER, measurement of ER and psychometric properties of ER measurements (reliability, validity, objectivity).
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly lists the additional variables sought for extraction and defines them (study/measurement characteristics, sample characteristics, ER definition/model, ER measurement and psychometric properties).
No explicit description was found of assumptions made about missing or unclear study information (e.g., how missing participant or study details were handled).

elements.quote: For data extraction, an a priori-developed tool was piloted on the first five articles.
elements.reason: The manuscript reports that an a priori-developed data extraction tool was used and piloted, but does not cite or otherwise identify a published or standardized tool or provide details allowing identification (no citation or name given).

elements.quote: For risk of bias ratings, study design-specific tools were used. The revised Cochrane Risk of Bias tool [227] was applied to randomized controlled trials, as it is specifically designed to evaluate internal validity in randomized designs. For non-randomized and observational quantitative studies, the Effective Public Health Practice Project (EPHPP) Quality Assessment Tool was used [232].
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly names the two risk-of-bias tools used (the revised Cochrane Risk of Bias tool/RoB 2 and the EPHPP Quality Assessment Tool).

elements.quote: In the EPHPP tool, domains are rated as strong, moderate, or weak and a global rating is assigned based on the number of weak domains. RoB 2 classifies studies as low risk, some concerns, or high risk, depending on the highest risk level across domains.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes how domains are rated and how global judgements are derived for both tools and names one specific RoB 2 domain later (see text_16). However, it does not provide a full list of the specific domains/components assessed by each tool.

elements.quote: In the EPHPP tool, domains are rated as strong, moderate, or weak and a global rating is assigned based on the number of weak domains. RoB 2 classifies studies as low risk, some concerns, or high risk, depending on the highest risk level across domains.
elements.reason: The manuscript reports that overall/global risk-of-bias judgements were made and specifies the rules used to derive them for both EPHPP (global based on number of weak domains) and RoB 2 (overall determined by the highest domain risk).

elements.quote: Within the EPHPP rating scheme, we excluded the 'Study Design' section, as it was not applicable to non-RCT studies.
elements.reason: An explicit adaptation to an existing tool (exclusion of the 'Study Design' section of the EPHPP tool) is described.
No evidence was found that a newly developed risk-of-bias tool was created or used in this review.

elements.quote: Risk of bias assessments were also conducted by the three authors (MB, RD, FS) and trained graduate students. Any discrepancies in ratings were discussed until consensus was reached.
elements.reason: The manuscript specifies who conducted risk-of-bias assessments (three named authors and trained graduate students), indicates multiple reviewers and that discrepancies were resolved through discussion and consensus; interrater agreement statistics are also reported in text_11 (Cohen's κ values).
No information is provided about processes used to obtain or confirm risk-of-bias information from study investigators (e.g., contacting study authors for clarification of bias-related items).
The manuscript provides no description of automation tools being used for risk-of-bias assessment (no use, training, performance, or validation details reported).

elements.quote: The primary outcome was the reporting of psychometric properties in behavioral and physiological ER measures. ... The proportion of studies reporting psychometric properties was estimated using a random-effects meta-analysis of logit-transformed proportions with inverse-variance weighting and Hartung-Knapp adjustment.
elements.reason: The manuscript specifies the outcome (reporting of psychometric properties) and the effect measure used for synthesis and presentation (proportions estimated via logit-transformed proportions meta-analysis).
No thresholds or ranges for interpreting effect sizes (e.g., cutoffs for small/medium/large) or a rationale for such thresholds are reported in the provided evidence.
The manuscript does not describe methods to re-express synthesized results using another effect measure in the provided excerpts.
Although the effect measure (proportions via logit transformation) is stated, no explicit justification for the choice of that effect measure is provided in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: Studies were included according to the PICOS criteria [177]. Eligible studies included participants from birth to 15 years and 11 months. Studies were required to use at least one ER measurement and report ER as an outcome variable. Both studies with and without group comparisons were eligible. No language restrictions were applied; studies in all languages were included. ... Studies reporting on secondary literature (e.g. meta-analyses, reviews) were excluded.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes explicit processes and criteria (PICOS-based eligibility, age range, required use of an ER measurement/outcome, inclusion of studies with/without group comparisons, language policy, and exclusion of secondary literature) used to determine which studies were eligible for inclusion and thus for synthesis.

elements.quote:
text_11: "Data preparation and descriptive statistics were conducted in IBM SPSS Statistics (version 29). Meta-analyses were performed in R (version 4.4.1) using the meta package (Fig. 2)."

text_9: "For data extraction, an a priori-developed tool was piloted on the first five articles. Extracted data comprised study identification, study and measurement characteristics (study design, publication type), sample characteristics (age, gender, ethnicity, child/family characteristics), definition/model of ER, measurement of ER and psychometric properties of ER measurements (reliability, validity, objectivity)."
elements.reason: The manuscript describes the data extraction items and the software used for data preparation and analysis, but it does not provide specific methods for preparing data for presentation or synthesis such as handling missing summary statistics, specific data conversions, imputation procedures, or rules for deriving effect estimates from reported statistics. Therefore the reporting is partial.

elements.quote: For each study, the minimum age at which the ER measurement was applied was used; if no minimum age was reported, the mean age was applied. Based on these values, measures were organized into broader age groups (neonates, infants, toddlers, preschool, school-aged children and teens) according to the American Academic of Pediatrics [6]. These broader categories were further divided into narrower age groups of 12 months categories. Within these 12 months categories the measures are organized according to the examined emotions (frustration/anger/disappointment, fear, jealousy, empathy, joy and non-specific emotion/mixed emotions). For the behavioral observations (Suppl. Mat., Table 1a - 1e), the task of how the emotion is triggered is described first, followed by the duration of this task, the coding manuals used to measure ER, information on reliability, validity and objectivity and the citations and number of studies using the emotion eliciting task. Specific coding manuals are not described for all tasks. The coding procedure can be found in the studies that use the emotion eliciting task. For the physiological measurements (Suppl. Mat., Table 2a - 2e), the measurement method (e.g. EEG, fMRI) is described first, followed by the measured physiological phenomenon, the emotion triggering tasks, information on reliability, validity and objectivity of the measured physiological phenomenon and the citations and number of studies measuring the physiological phenomenon.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly describes the tabular structures in the Supplementary Material and the data fields included for behavioral observation and physiological measurement tables (ordering by age groups, emotion categories, task details, reliability/validity/objectivity, citations).

elements.quote: As shown in Fig. 3, studies focusing on younger age groups predominantly used behavioral observation measures, whereas studies involving older age groups favored physiological measurements.
elements.reason: While figures are referenced (e.g., Fig. 3), there is no description of the graphical methods used to display results (no description of plot types, axes, visual encoding, or software/methods for graphs). Therefore the methods used to create graphical displays are not reported in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: For each study, the minimum age at which the ER measurement was applied was used; if no minimum age was reported, the mean age was applied. Based on these values, measures were organized into broader age groups (neonates, infants, toddlers, preschool, school-aged children and teens) according to the American Academic of Pediatrics [6]. These broader categories were further divided into narrower age groups of 12 months categories. Within these 12 months categories the measures are organized according to the examined emotions (frustration/anger/disappointment, fear, jealousy, empathy, joy and non-specific emotion/mixed emotions).
elements.reason: The manuscript states the basis for ordering studies in tables (minimum/mean age used to assign studies to age groups, then 12-month bins, then grouped by examined emotions).

No evidence is provided describing use of non-standard graphs or the rationale for using them; the manuscript does not report any rationale for non-standard graphical displays in the retrieved evidence.
No software package name or version is reported in the retrieved methods text. The methods describe the meta-analytic approach but do not state which software or packages (and versions) were used.

elements.quote: Pooled effect estimates for specific reliability or validity indices were not calculated, as the available data were limited to the subset of studies reporting these psychometric indices (61% of all 516 studies). Because the reporting of such indices was not systematic across the literature, the resulting dataset may not have been fully representative of the broader evidence base. Consequently, any pooled estimates derived from this subset may have been biased and could potentially overestimate the true effects.
elements.reason: The authors explicitly state that pooled estimates for specific indices were not calculated and justify this decision by explaining limited, non-systematic reporting and potential bias in the subset of studies.

elements.quote: The proportion of studies reporting psychometric properties was estimated using a random-effects meta-analysis of logit-transformed proportions with inverse-variance weighting and Hartung-Knapp adjustment.
elements.reason: The meta-analysis model is reported (random-effects meta-analysis of logit-transformed proportions), but no explicit rationale is provided for choosing this model.

elements.quote: The proportion of studies reporting psychometric properties was estimated using a random-effects meta-analysis of logit-transformed proportions with inverse-variance weighting and Hartung-Knapp adjustment.
elements.reason: The statistical method (logit-transformed proportions, inverse-variance weighting, Hartung-Knapp adjustment) used for the meta-analysis is explicitly described.

elements.quote: Heterogeneity was assessed using Cochran's Q and the I 2 statistic.
elements.reason: Methods used to identify/quantify heterogeneity (Cochran's Q and I2) are explicitly reported.
Although a random-effects meta-analysis is reported, the between-study variance estimator (e.g., DerSimonian-Laird, REML) is not specified in the retrieved text.

elements.quote: The proportion of studies reporting psychometric properties was estimated using a random-effects meta-analysis of logit-transformed proportions with inverse-variance weighting and Hartung-Knapp adjustment.
elements.reason: The authors report using the Hartung-Knapp adjustment, which describes the method used to calculate/adjust confidence intervals for the summary effect in the random-effects meta-analysis.

No additional implementation details for the random-effects model (e.g., weighting details beyond inverse-variance, convergence criteria, or estimation settings) are provided in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: However, this review has several limitations that should be considered when interpreting the findings. First, the restricted age range, which was necessary for feasibility, limits the generalizability of our conclusions regarding ER measurements in adolescents, as the focus is primarily on younger age groups. Second, the review excluded questionnaire-based methods to enhance readability, meaning that our analysis of psychometric properties is confined to behavioral observation and physiological measurement methods, which may omit relevant insights from self-report instruments. Third, the available data on psychometric properties were limited to a subset of studies, as a considerable proportion of studies did not report any psychometric information. Consequently, the analyses of psychometric properties are based on a selective subset of the literature, which may not be fully representative of all studies. Our analyses indicate systematic differences between studies that report psychometric properties and those that do not, particularly by measurement type and age groups, suggesting that reporting reflects study characteristics rather than consistent measurement standards. Fourth, the characteristics of the underlying study populations introduce further constraints. Consistent with the WEIRD problem in psychological science [213], most studies provided limited information on ethnicity or household income (Table 1). When reported, samples were predominantly White, and few studies included participants from low-income families (Table 1). Because ER strategies vary across cultural and socioeconomic contexts, the lack of diverse samples limits the generalizability and applicability of the findings [64, 68, 200, 201]. Fifth, the clinical scope of the included studies is narrow. Most investigations focused on healthy children, with only a small proportion examining psychological disorders (Table 1). Internalizing disorders, which often co-occur with externalizing disorders, were underrepresented despite their prevalence and early onset, particularly in the case of anxiety disorders [24, 151]. Consequently, the current evidence provides a limited view of the psychometric quality and applicability of ER measurement methods in clinical populations.
elements.reason: The Limitations section explicitly discusses multiple limitations of the included evidence (age range, exclusion of questionnaires, incomplete reporting of psychometrics, sample demographics/WEIRD bias, and limited clinical scope), directly addressing the checklist item.

elements.quote: This review highlights several gaps in the literature on ER measurements, suggesting directions for future research. One important consideration is the need to more carefully specify the underlying definitions and theoretical models of ER being examined. Clearer conceptual grounding may help guiding the selection, application, and interpretation of measurement methods. In this context, further efforts toward greater consistency in measurement approaches may be beneficial. For example, more systematic alignment in the choice of behavioral observation tasks, physiological indicators, and reporting practices supports comparability across studies. ... Future research should therefore adopt more standardized measurement and reporting practices, including the routine reporting of reliability and validity indices. In addition, most behavioral observation and physiological measurement studies have predominantly focused on negative emotions, with comparatively less attention given to the regulation of positive emotions. Expanding research in this area is important, as positive emotions are a central aspect of ER, linked to mental health and well-being, and are relevant in social relationships [50, 80]. Beyond the characteristics of individual measures, combining multiple ER assessment methods provides a more comprehensive perspective on regulatory processes. Likewise, most studies focus on healthy children or externalizing disorders, leaving evidence on internalizing and other clinically relevant conditions comparatively sparse. Addressing these gaps enhances the applicability of ER measurement methods and deepens our understanding of emotional development and psychopathology.
elements.reason: The 'Implications For Future Research' section gives explicit, concrete recommendations for future studies (e.g., specify theoretical models, standardize measurement and reporting, routinely report reliability and validity, study positive emotions, combine multiple assessment methods, include internalizing and clinical populations).
